Validation · immersed-boundary conjugate heat transfer

Conjugate heat transfer in turbulent pipe flow, against body-fitted DNS

A Cartesian volume-penalization solver with a level-set conjugate interface, measured against Neuhauser's spectral-element thermal DNS at Reτ = 181, Pr = 0.71 — seven thermal boundary conditions on one velocity field. Comparison figures show the finest grid (Δ⁺ 1.84, Δz⁺ 5.06); the four-grid resolution study is §9.

§1 Why this case

Every previous validation of this solver's conjugate scheme used a flat, grid-aligned interface — Flageul's channel, the manufactured slab problems — where the cut-face coefficient reduces to the textbook two-resistance harmonic mean and is exact. A pipe is the first curved conjugate interface: cut cells take arbitrary level-set weights, the wall is a staircase in the Cartesian mesh, and the solver's own manufactured convergence test measures the scheme as first order there. This campaign asks what that costs in a turbulence result, and whether the error behaves as discretisation error should.

The pipe is streamwise-periodic, D = 1, Lz = 12.5 D, with a conjugate shell 0.5 < r < 0.6 and an insulated jacket beyond. It is driven by the pressure gradient built from Neuhauser's measured friction velocity, so uτ = 0.068379 by construction and Reb is an outcome, not an input. Heat is generated in the fluid by the streamwise (Kasagi) reduction and removed by a volumetric sink in the shell.

§2 The seven cases

The dataset's (K, λsf) map to the solver as κs/κf = λsf and ρcs/ρcf = 1/(K²λsf), K being the fluid-to-solid effusivity ratio. All seven ride one velocity field, so every comparison between them is at the same turbulence realisation.

c1 and c2 are the only cases carrying a conductivity contrast, and are therefore the real test of the conjugate face coefficient — it is a conductivity harmonic mean and is the identity when κs = κf, whatever the capacity does.

§3 Two methodological findings

Both changed the answers, and both generalise beyond this case.

Finding 1

A source/sink imbalance the mean profile hides can dominate a time-averaged variance

Sizing the shell sink from the continuum u_b = 1 leaves a 2.79 % imbalance, because the discrete ∫u_z dV gives ub = 0.9755. The field then cools uniformly at 0.267 per unit time. The mean is immune — a uniform ramp cancels when the profile is referenced to the interface — but the drift adds a variance ~(λT)²/12 that is spatially uniform, hence worst where the true fluctuation is smallest: θ′ came out +32 % high at the axis, falling to +11 % at y⁺ 42. Because λ ∝ 1/Ctotal it biases each scalar differently, which inverted the conductivity sweep. Single snapshots carry no time average and showed the true values, which is what pinned the diagnosis rather than leaving it an argument. Size the sink from the discrete generation the solver actually applies.

Finding 2

θτ must come from the heat balance, not from a near-wall slope

A slope differenced across the cut cells reads 6.6 % low on the coarse grid and 0.0 % low on the fine one. Normalising by it flatters the coarse grid, cancelling a too-small temperature scale against a too-low profile — it reported the mean as "+0.6 %" where the honest figure is −6.0 %. All wall units here use qw = |Q|/(2πRL) from the interface-heat diagnostic, which is well-conditioned on either grid.

An exact law needing no reference data: integrating the axial momentum balance of a steady, fully developed pipe once gives −ν d⟨uz⟩/dr + ⟨ur′uz′⟩ = uτ²r/R. Measured deviation max 2.3 %, mean 0.68 % of uτ², which confirms both statistical convergence and that the immersed wall delivers the stress it is driven with. With r from the axis the mean shear is negative, so the down-gradient Reynolds stress is positive and adds to the viscous term — the opposite of the channel convention.

§7 Turbulent heat fluxes

§8 The instantaneous field

One cross-section of the fine-grid solution: the three velocity components and the pressure, then the seven scalars as fluctuations about their own azimuthal mean.

All seven scalars ride the same velocity field, so their fluid structure is identical by construction, and the panel set becomes a direct picture of the measurement. K = 4, the least effusive solid, carries the deepest penetration into the shell; K = 0.25 the shallowest; MBC's shell is exactly blank, because the Dirichlet body holds the body value to the last bit, and its near-wall fluid fluctuation is visibly damped.

Inspection finding

Three things the instantaneous field exposed — two of them defects in this analysis

(i) A speckle at the pipe axis: the figure's fault. The azimuthal mean was taken on radial rings of fixed width, 0.0012 = 0.24 cells. A ring that thin holds no cells at all near the axis, so the subtracted mean was interpolated through empty bins and the residual was the raw field. Fixed by adapting the ring width, w(r) = max(wmin, NΔ²/2πr) with N = 64: the axis residual drops from 3.08 to 1.45, matching its neighbours.

(ii) A bright ring at the shell/jacket boundary — also the figure's fault, and it corrupted a measurement reported here. A ring straddling r = 0.6 mixes shell cells with inert jacket cells held at a constant value, so its azimuthal mean is meaningless: the residual there is 667 units against 4–6 inside the isoflux shell. That ring sat inside the band used for the "solid, outer half" artifact below, and a fixed ring narrower than a cell also aliases the azimuths — which, because cells at a given radius have four-fold symmetry, lands on m = 4, 8, 12, exactly where a Cartesian artifact would.

(iii) The isoflux modulation is real — characterised below — and (iv) it exposed a defect in the rms definition that inflated every solid-side fluctuation in this report by up to 113 %.

The claim that the F2 band boundary carries a distinctly larger artifact than the rest of the solid was wrong — it was the jacket ring in the measurement. The outer half carries the same ~0.9 % as everywhere else and converges with it. The cut-cell and inner-solid figures are unaffected.

The isoflux shell modulation

A radial cut through that shell alternates cell to cell (−1.50, +1.53, −0.16, +1.62 in units of the fluid's own fluctuation) where c0 decays smoothly (−1.18, −0.84, −0.52, −0.30). It is not an azimuthal high-frequency mode: the spectrum peaks at m = 8, 6, 12 and carries only 16 % of its energy above m = 128, where cell scale would be m ≈ 337.

Table 7. Cell-scale content of the residual in the first three solid cells.
caseκsamplitude% of that shell's ΔTconverges?
c0 / c1 / c21 / 2 / 0.50.24 / 0.24 / 0.28~0.4 %no — it is resolved turbulence, not error
isoflux0.014.450.10 %order 1.85 (10.62 → 4.45)

It is steady, not growing (4.39 → 4.47 → 4.45 over t = 87…150, so not an instability), decays with depth (4.45 → 4.15 → 1.83 over cells 0–3, 3–8, 8–18), and converges at order 1.85. It is the staircase imprinting a cell-to-cell variation of the local flux on the solid's time-mean field. For the normal-conductivity cases the equivalent number is not an artifact at all but ordinary resolved turbulence imprinted on the solid, which is why it does not converge.

And it is not anomalous for the isoflux case. Steady conduction in the solid obeys ∇·(κs∇T) = 0, so κs cancels from the shape of the field and only scales its amplitude. Against each case's own shell temperature drop the isoflux modulation is the smallest of the seven — 0.11 %, against c1's 1.18 %, c0's 0.59 % and c2's 0.35 %. It looks pathological in Figure 7 only because every panel there is normalised by the fluid's fluctuation, common to all seven, while the isoflux solid's own scale is 100× larger.

The actual fix

What the modulation corrupted was the definition of θ′, not the solution

A steady azimuthal pattern contributes nothing to a temporal fluctuation, but it does contribute to a variance formed from bin-averaged moments — which is what this analysis computed: rmsbin² = ⟨temporal variance⟩ + Varazimuthal(time mean). The second term is the staircase imprint, and unlike a fluctuation it does not decay with depth. Measured inflation of the solid-side θ′: 22–36 % (c0), 11–17 % (c3), 72–113 % (isoflux).

Recomputed as the per-cell temporal rms averaged over the bin — the reference's own definition — the fine-grid solid profile moves from 20–23 % high to within 0.3–3 % of the DNS at every depth (§6.1). That also disposes of a suspected limitation: the fine solid profile was never carrying its interpolated initial condition.

If the solid field itself is wanted pointwise, the levers on the modulation are, in order of cost: refine (it converges at order 1.85); relax the contrast — the isoflux control does not require ε = 0.01, and since the interface response saturates in K, ε = 0.1 would cut the solid's temperature scale tenfold at some cost in fidelity to the K → ∞ limit; or regularise the cut-cell arm fraction (an area-weighted face coefficient, clamping w, or merging small solid cut cells) — but the C2 increment measured area-weighting to be worse for the flux, so any such change needs its own gate.

The axial spacing controls the fluid turbulence, and the production grid proves it the only way possible — by varying the other direction alone. Halving Δ⁺ at fixed Δz⁺ = 5.1 moves the fluid-side errors by ≤ 0.5 percentage points; halving Δz⁺ at fixed Δ⁺ moves the core deficit from −16.6 % to −6.0 %. The original two-grid study refined Δ⁺ by 1.60× but Δz⁺ by only 1.40×, so it could not separate the directions and left the aspect ratio slightly worse (4.81 → 5.49). Its "second-order convergence" is therefore convergence in Δz⁺, not Δ⁺, and the core deficit was never slow convergence — it was a direction barely refined.

The radial spacing controls the solid side, which axial refinement cannot help because conduction into the shell is a radial problem: the z-fine grid is the worst there, while the two grids resolving the penetration depth with 3.6 cells rather than 2.3 reproduce the shell decay to 1–2 %.

And the solid excess was a normalisation

The conjugate scheme reproduces the penetration essentially exactly

Every grid read the shell decay +5…+9 % high when normalised by the value at the interface — but that bin is a CUT CELL, whose penalization blend under-represents θ′ and so inflates every ratio below it. Normalised one cell deeper, at (r−R)/d = 0.1, the fine grid reproduces the decay to −0.2 … −1.2 % and the production grid to +0.1 … +2.3 %. What the earlier numbers measured was the cut cell in the denominator, not the physics — and the penetration through the solid is the measurement this campaign exists for.

Δ⁺ ≈ 1 is not reachable here, and the reason is worth recording: at Δz⁺ 5 it needs 206 M cells and 80 GB against this card's 32.6 GB, and because the conjugate Peclet limit scales with the radial spacing squared, the same window would take 354 h. The production grid is the largest that fits.

Mechanism

Why the axial spacing set the core variance

The ⟨θ′²⟩ budget closes on both sides (residual ≤ 0.02 against terms up to 0.34), and at the axis production is zero: the core variance is sustained entirely by turbulent transport from the wall region, balanced by dissipation. That is the term the coarse grid was losing — transport ratio 0.36 at y⁺ 110 — and refining z restored it to 0.91, with the variance following from 0.74 to 0.94. The transport is carried by large-scale, strongly z-elongated events, which is why the axial spacing and not the dissipation range set it. Our resolved dissipation per unit variance was only 3 % high at the axis while the variance was 31 % low: a scaled-down cascade in balance, not an over-dissipative scheme.

At this boundary condition the flow is axisymmetric, so azimuthal structure in the statistics is ours — an error measure no body-fitted code can report. At the wall the m = 4 amplitude is 0.94 % of the wall-to-axis temperature difference on the coarse grid, seven times its noise floor, and falls into the floor of the fine grid's shorter window. The solid carries the same magnitude throughout its depth (0.92 % inner, 0.86 % outer) — see Table 6, whose earlier version put the outer half at 4.75 % through a measurement defect.

§10 Limitations

  1. Averaging window. 600 D/ub (coarse), 200 (fine and z-fine) against Neuhauser's ≈ 4400 — less of a limitation than it looks: in their own data the slow, between-batch content is 0.2–1.4 % of the variance and smallest at the axis, so ~200 D/ub already captures 99.8 % of the core variance, and our leg-to-leg scatter is ±2 %. The artifact floor, a spatial-residual measure, does remain window-limited.
  2. The Cartesian-artifact measure is not grid-independent. The m = 4 amplitude in the band y⁺ 0.04–3.6 reads 0.94 % (coarse), 0.45 % (fine), 0.19 % (z-fine), 1.28 % (production) — not a convergent sequence, because that band holds one cut-cell layer on the coarse grids and a cut layer plus a full fluid layer on the finest. It is neither noise (floors 0.14–0.39 %) nor a transient (production halves 1.19 and 0.97 %, solid mean drifting 0.05 %). Quote it per grid; the convergence rate previously claimed for it is withdrawn.
  3. The fine grid started from the interpolated coarse field, to avoid repeating transients that cost ~9× more there. The suspicion that its solid-side profile still carried the coarse penetration proved unfounded — that discrepancy was the rms definition (§8 iv). A continuation leg is doubling its window regardless.
  4. The cut cell is not a point. Everything inside y⁺ ≈ 3 is a penalization blend over a cell that straddles the wall; comparing it pointwise with a body-fitted DNS is not like-for-like. This is what limits the MBC control.
  5. The shell's outer surface is a staircase at ±h/2, i.e. d = 0.1 ± 2.8 % azimuthally on the coarse grid.
  6. Pr = 0.71 and azimuthally uniform heating only. The dataset's Pr = 0.025 would make the scalar diffusion limit dominate the time step; the sinusoidal heating cases need an azimuthally varying immersed flux.
